text: Quantum machine learning sits at the intersection of two fields that are each already hard on their own, and gluing them together does not automatically produce something better than either alone. This course treats QML as a legitimate, active research area, not a shipped technology with proven advantages.

Quantum machine learning is an umbrella term covering at least four different research threads. First, quantum algorithms that speed up classical ML subroutines like matrix inversion or PCA. Second, variational circuits used as trainable classifiers, this course's main focus. Third, quantum kernel methods, where the quantum computer only measures a similarity value that gets handed to a classical support vector machine. And fourth, quantum-native ML, which analyzes data that is itself quantum rather than classical data.

Today's quantum hardware is the real constraint. A circuit you can actually run has on the order of tens of qubits and limited depth before noise overwhelms the signal. Deeper, more expressive circuits accumulate more error per layer, creating a direct tension between expressiveness and noise. Nothing in this course runs on fault-tolerant, error-corrected hardware, because that hardware doesn't exist yet at useful scale.

Theoretically interesting and practically advantageous are different claims. Provable quantum speedups exist for carefully constructed mathematical problems, and those proofs are real. But as of today there is no peer-reviewed, independently reproduced demonstration of a quantum ML method beating the best classical approach on a real, messy, practical task. We learn this anyway for research literacy, transferable skills in parameterized circuits and gradient estimation, and early positioning if a genuine advantage is ever found.
Next lesson recaps the classical machine learning pipeline, features, model, loss, and optimizer, so every later comparison to a quantum version has a fair, specific baseline to measure against.
